idiom_name: tokio reactor plus tokio::task::spawn_blocking (or std threads and std::sync::mpsc)
implementation_notes: Tokio provides the asynchronous layer as its reactor, which demultiplexes readiness and drives async tasks, and it provides the synchronous layer explicitly: spawn_blocking runs a closure on a dedicated pool meant for blocking work that would otherwise stall a runtime worker. The queueing layer is tokio::sync::mpsc when the hand-off happens from async code, or std::sync::mpsc with plain std::thread workers when there is no async runtime and the front end is already thread-based. Keep the classic structure where the blocked work is unavoidable (blocking database drivers, compression, crypto); otherwise a pure async pipeline is simpler.
pitfalls: spawn_blocking closures must be 'static and own their data; holding a MutexGuard or a borrowed reference across the hand-off re-imports blocking into the async layer.
The blocking pool is bounded (max_blocking_threads, 512 by default): a blocking storm queues inside the pool and adds latency silently instead of failing.
Calling blocking std::fs or a synchronous database driver from an async task does not raise an error - it just stalls the reactor under load.
Cancelling the awaiting future does not stop a blocking closure that is already running on the blocking pool.
